utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May I remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, yes, that's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Momcilo Bulatovic, I am attorney-at-law, one of Defence counsel of Mr. Sljivancanin, and I will be putting questions on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin's team to you. I will make sure that my questions are brief and clear so that you can provide answers that are similar to that and we can conclude as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since I want to start with a number of questions that could compromise the identity of the witness, could we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us about your superior. What I want to know is did you report to your superior on any assignments completed once orders had been received and how did you do this, orally, did you submit written reports, did you submit interim reports or just regular ones? I want to know everything.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about my superior during combat or my superior in terms of the establishment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about both.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the combat activities I was at the front line with the commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment, Major Bajic, only. I was company commander at the time, and I was involved in our daily reporting, in our reports to the barracks which was the command post of the commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment. These were regular daily reports, perhaps not every single day. Most of these had to do with events along the front line, any problems that were occurring, and how to deal with those. The usual things that one tends to talk about at a time like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. During the fighting and also in terms of the establishment, who would have been in a position, who would have had the power to issue you an order? Your superior only?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chain of subordination in the guards brigade was a well-known fact, and this applied to all other JNA units or perhaps to any army across the world. The chain of command is established, and everybody knows how an order travels, up and down the chain of command, all the way down to ordinary soldiers. Since this was a special unit, it was not a classic unit in the usual sense of the word, the units of which I was commander.(redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you not to mention the specific unit, because you are revealing your own identity. I wanted to remain in public session, so please do not refer openly to your own position. I'm talking about the principles. Who can issue you an order? Your superior or someone else as well? Who would have had the power to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for stepping in. I wanted to say this: We were not a text-book unit, if you like. And we received our assignments from a number of different sources, purely technical assignments down the chain of command. These assignments tended to be very specific. They concerned military security, primarily. We would be given these assignments by the security organ, therefore it could have been the case that I received an order from the security officer, but also from someone higher up, the brigade commander or the chief of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In a situation like this, for example you receiving an order from someone who is not your direct superior, would you not be duty-bound to inform your direct superior either of the fact that you have received an order, or upon completion of a given task?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depended, especially in the 1990 -- in 1990 and 1991, on the urgency of an assignment. There were times when I was not duty-bound to inform anyone about an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Which type of assignment are we talking about, just give us one example where you were not duty-bound to inform your commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me, and you were the one who just told me a minute ago that we were in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's a good idea. Can we please go into closed session for the witness's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Closed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would now like to ask the usher to give a paper to the witness, and also a pencil, so that the witness could draw for us, based on his recollections, the hangars that he mentioned, the bus and the location of the bus, which way did the bus face, the lights that were on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you'd better be specific in what you want, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the witness draw for us the hangar that he saw when he was at Ovcara on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that night?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... drawing, not a sketch of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely right. I don't think the witness has these capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So can you please draw for us the road that you travelled on, the position of the hangar in relation to the road, and also the position of that one bus that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will attempt to do that, based on my recollections. I will try to sketch the micro-location where one will be able to see the hangar and the opening or rather the door through which I saw the prisoners. Now, as to my capabilities, I think we can discuss it on another occasion. [Marks]. I attempted to do something here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Where we see the arrow, I suppose that that denotes the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to us the direction from which you came? I assume that that was the direction of the arrow. You so were travelling from Vukovar in which direction? Where does this road take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you interested in the micro-location of the hangar or in the broader area of the topographic map?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm only interested in decoding what you drew here. You came from the direction of the arrow, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And what is that direction, is it Vukovar going to where? Is it to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. You were not entirely clear in your first question. That road was a narrow road, the field road. And at some point it joined the road between Vukovar and Negoslavci. And then right here once again it joined another road, also leading to Vukovar, which was closer to the Danube, so to speak. [Marks]. In my assessment, I came from this direction, and I returned in that direction too. As to the distance between these two spots, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This square here, I assume that that's the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the rectangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the rectangle. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I also drew something additional here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can guess what it is. Can you mark that rectangle number one so we can identify it as the hangar. Please put number 1 and circle it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This vehicle here right next to the entrance into the hangar, I assume that that's the jeep in which you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the jeeps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put number two there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The third rectangle with these lines in front, I suppose denotes the bus with the lights on, and the bus is facing forward. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please put number three there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: These dots on the left side of the rectangle, I suppose are the people that you saw in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. These are small circles. And then the dots represent the line, or rather the rope that was stretched in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please put number four there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And the opening, I suppose, is the entrance. Would you please put number five if I'm correct, and if this is indeed the entrance into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what's the distance from the entrance into the hangar marked with number five to the front of the bus with the lights on marked with number three? So what's the distance between the lights of the bus to the hangar entrance, based on your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's possible that the distance was between five and 10 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the bus headlights, did you also see any other lights in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now pointing to the symbol here, which denotes a lamp and the direction in which that lamp shone. And -- and this part of the hangar with the lines was the part where I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please mark this lamp in the hangar with number six?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 558.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. Since it was dark and we didn't stay there long, it's possible that if we rotate this hangar by 90 degrees, then it would face the road in this way. I can't confirm this with certainty, but as far as I can remember I approached it from this direction, and the door was on my right side. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you whether there was just one hangar or more than one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question? You mean you're asking me that directly? What I saw at that moment was this door and this hangar. I didn't look around, because it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, if you can remember: How far was this bus from the road? So what's the distance between the right side of the bus and the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I would be speculating if I were to tell you anything. One to five or ten metres. It was facing this way, I didn't realise at the time that this sort of information would one day be helpful. Don't get me wrong, please, but right now I am unable to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What you do remember, beyond a shadow of a doubt, is that the bus was facing the entrance to the hangar like this, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the initial portion to your statement where you talked about the one to three buses, as you say. What sort of an area was that, the surface, I mean. Was it a grass surface, a concrete surface, dirt? Where was this bus parked, on what sort of surface?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already pointed out on account of poor lighting and on account of me not paying attention to that, I am unable to say what was around the bus. It just wasn't something that I was focusing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So you lingered for about 15 minutes and then you headed back. At one point you heard sounds of firing, shots being fired. If I read your statement correctly, you couldn't tell exactly where this was coming from, but the distance must have been several hundred metres, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this now: When you heard these sounds of firing what was the first thought that occurred to you? What was the first thing that you associated with these sounds, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anything specific sprang to mind in connection with the firing, but we left the possibility open that this was a case of celebratory fire, which was something that was quite rife in the area at the time. As for the direction or the area that the firing was coming from, the area in which these shots were being fired, it's not something that I'm able to specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to your non-commissioned officers about this firing? Did you comment or did you not comment just because you put this down to some sort of celebratory fire which was a daily occurrence in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether we, in fact, exchanged comments about this particular firing. I'm sorry, shall we be requiring this sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will be tendering that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, we can take the ELMO away now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think 15 or 20 minutes will do, Your Honours. If that's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be run over the tape, unfortunately. It's a question of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's no problem to have a break now, and then to continue after the break, and then 15 or 20 minutes will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will need to break for half an hour because of the redaction. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I've been looking at some of my questions during the break and some of your answers too. Just in order to clarify some details. You talked about that assignment when some officers were seconded to the security administration. You talked about an assignment, I'll be mentioning it. We're in public session. Did you have any other such assignments where officers were seconded to the security administration? Just say yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is it necessary for you to describe the specific assignment, do you think we should go into private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've mentioned that already. That was in the autumn of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's the one that we were discussing, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Any other assignments that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a group comprising 10 young officers who were attached to the cabinet of the federal secretary for All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me if I say that in situations like these where a necessity arises for a group of officers to be seconded to the security administration, the procedure to follow is the following: The chief of the security administration sends a request to the brigade commander for a number of officers to be seconded to the security administration for a particular assignment. The company commander and the battalion commander are informed about this, but approval is granted by the brigade commander. Would that not seem to be the correct procedure to follow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure you have just described may be the procedure that is actually applied in cases like these, but that was above my head, so to speak. I didn't really know for sure. I do accept this as a possibility though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the decision of the OG South commander dated the 16th of November detaching you from the assault detachment and sending you back to your original unit, the military police battalion? Have you ever seen that decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in writing. However, believe me, I can't say for sure. It is certainly possible. I do apologise. I know that in those days before or after I was in touch with Captain Susic. That much is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since 1996, which is when you provided your statement to the OTP, had you given any other statements to anyone up until May about these events that we are discussing here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I gave a statement to the OTP investigators back in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that statement I gave another one, which is the present annex to my statement, and that happened quite recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you provided that annex to your statement, how many days did you spend in The Hague on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said recently. I got it mixed up slightly. When I say recently, I mean two or three years ago. I spent a couple of days here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Witness, would you be kind enough please to look at your supplementary note that you made. Does it have a date at the bottom with your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just need to clarify one thing, if Your Honour would forgive me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you look at the English translation, would you mind? To see if you see your signature there. If not, we will have it on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-001 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have it. I don't have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at your screen, please. Now, we will have to go into private session, because clearly the signature is -- or we will submit the signature is there. So could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please take the card and read out the affirmation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, could you state your full name and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Zlatko Zlogledja, I was born on the 19th of March, 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In 1991 did you join the JNA as part of your national service?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what date did you join?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The 17th of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you train for before you were given an assignment, a military assignment?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was your first military assignment in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: First there was the training, and then we were told that we would be going to Slovenia, when ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After you were told that you were going to Slovenia, did, in fact, you go there, or were you assigned somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: We didn't. We left Valjevo, we left the barracks, and stopped near a power plant at Sabac, and that was where we set up camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then in late August, early September, 1991, were you assigned to combat activities in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And briefly can you state the position that you took, or where your unit was positioned in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: We were positioned at Negoslavci, and from Negoslavci towards Luzac, which is a suburb of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Briefly can you describe the size of the unit you were assigned to, the number of men, and the type of equipment, military equipment, vehicles, et cetera, that were assigned to your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: There were about 20 tanks stationed there, and military APCs, as well as about 100 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how far from the centre of Vukovar, the centre of the town, was your unit positioned, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: We were in that field just outside the suburb itself, outside Luzac. It was quite far from the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were located at this position, what were your duties within the unit?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: While we were located at this position, our duties were to dig trenches. We were told to be careful and to guard the trenches. Because otherwise the enemy might sneak in on us, and that was why we had to be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Approximately what length of time did you stay with this unit at this position?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I stayed for about four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after that four or five days, what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: After that four or five days I decided with another four fellow soldiers to escape to Vukovar, to escape into free territory. It was becoming quite obvious that we would have to use our weapons sooner or later, which meant that I would have to start firing at my own people, in my case. I decided to have no part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who did you decide to escape with?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Srecko Ravlija, Samir Hrkic, Dodaj Hajdar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The other person Lorenc Duhanaj?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: And Lorenc Duhanaj, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you -- how did you escape and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Lorenc Duhanaj was a local. He was from Marinci. He knew the area well. We agreed that he would take us across to Luzac, and on to the Vukovar police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was your escape plan, was it to assist in the defence of the town or was it to leave the town completely?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The plan was to abandon our positions and to each go back to our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Why did you decide to head for the Vukovar police station?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Simply because that was the only way, and this was the only road leading into Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you got to the police station, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: They checked us there, who we were and where we had come from. Having been vetted, we were given a chance to call our families. However, I called my aunt in Zagreb, since my folks back home did not own a phone. My aunt told me that my family were staying with them in Zagreb because my own village had already been taken by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Once you received that news what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: As all of my mates decided to stay and join the police reserve forces, I too decided to join them and help with the town's defence, to try and keep Vukovar from meeting the same kind of fate as my own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you given any particular job in this defence of the town by the commander of the police or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: At first we just helped out at the station. Later on, when things became complicated and when everything got serious, we too were sent to the front line to give them a hand there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at one point in time did you decide to leave Vukovar completely?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain why you made that decision, and when that was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The road was blocked, and Vukovar was cut off. It was impossible to leave, and I had no choice but to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But when did you attempt to leave the town? Was it when Vukovar was about to fall? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: That was on the eve of Vukovar's fall. I tried to escape with a group of other people. As we were trying to make our way out of Vukovar, Lorenc Duhanaj stepped on a mine. We then had to walk all the way back to Vukovar Hospital to leave him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you stay at Vukovar Hospital for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: When we left Lorenc there, I decided that I too would be staying. I stayed at the hospital for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After taking Lorenc to the hospital, why did you decide to stay there for those few days?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: This was on the eve of the fall of Vukovar. This was the very end, if you like. I felt that this was the safest place for me to be at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What date did you leave the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I left the hospital on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We'll talk about what happened when you left the hospital in a moment, but if you take can your mind back to the night before, what happened the night before you left the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The hospital was surrounded by the Serbian forces. Serb soldiers were entering the hospital and taking people away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say Serb soldiers, can you be a little more specific as to whether they were regular JNA soldiers, reserve JNA soldiers, paramilitaries, or armed Serb people, if you can? Or a combination?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: There were local Serbs there, as well as JNA soldiers, reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that these Serbian forces were taking people away on the night before, about how many people are you talking about, and who were they?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Specifically I remember this one thing, I remember a Serb soldier approaching me asking me where I was from. At the time it occurred to me to answer that I was a local, I thought that was the best thing for me to say. There was a police officer from Vukovar standing next to me, Zoran, we called him Baki, whom this Serbian soldier recognised, I think they were even related. He then took him away. I know that he didn't want to go because he had been wounded in his arm, and he said so. He said he was unable to leave, and yet the soldier took him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to this Zoran?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: No. The soldier later returned, and took another man away, a young lad called Rasid. He was Zoran's friend. He took him away, too, and I never heard what became of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can look at what happened on the morning of the 20th of November, 1991. You testified that you left the hospital on that day. Can you tell us how you left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: That morning, sometime between 8.00 and 9.00, we were told that the buses were there, that we were all to leave the hospital, which we did. We stood outside the hospital and lined up, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who told you that the buses were there and you were to leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you stood outside the hospital and you lined up. Did someone order you to line up, or did people just line up of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes, we were ordered to line up. They frisked us too, for any belongings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who ordered to you line up, and who was doing the frisking?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The Serb military police were there, the Serb reservists probably from Serbia, as well as local Serbs from Vukovar, natives who were also wearing JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many of these soldiers were there outside of the hospital near this line-up and where the frisking was occurring?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Quite many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did anyone appear to be in charge of these soldiers to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was that or who were they?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I saw a man wearing a camouflage uniform. He was in and out of the hospital all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This man wearing the camouflage uniform, can you describe him more specifically in terms of his height, perhaps his build, and whether he was wearing anything, his face.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: He was quite tall, black hair, and a black moustache. Of solid build.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did this man have any facial hair?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Just the moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about any hat, helmet, or was he wearing nothing on his head, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform and a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What type of cap was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: A camouflage one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the build, what type of build was he? Thin, fat, solid or any other?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: He was slender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you know that person's name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How did you know his name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: While we were still in the Vukovar police building we were able to watch TV. We watched Serb reports from their TV stations. I saw him there, on their TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How often did you see him on the TV, and can you describe the context in which you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: We were able to follow their programmes. I saw him several times. He was lending moral support to his soldiers, saying that they would have no trouble at all dealing with the Croatian forces, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You stated that you saw him at the hospital on the morning of the 20th. When you saw him on TV, was that the -- before the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After you left the hospital did you ever see Sljivancanin again in person?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: After I left the hospital I saw him again at Ovcara, but that was the only time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You say that you saw him at Ovcara. When was that? Was that on the same day or another day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can go back to what happened at the Vukovar Hospital in the morning on the 20th, you said that you were lined up and you were frisked. When you say you were lined up, what other people were lined up with you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: All those slightly wounded who were still able to walk were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After you were frisked, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: When the frisking was done we headed for the buses. We entered the buses, we got on to the buses and we set out. We stopped at the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many buses went to the Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: A total of four or five buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the bus that you were on, was anyone guarding it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes. There was an armed Serb soldier watching us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was he -- are you able to say whether he was reserve soldier or a regular soldier or a paramilitary or simply an armed civilian?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: He was their military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What happened when you got to Vukovar barracks, if you can briefly explain.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: When the buses stopped in front of the Vukovar barracks we were met once again by Serb soldiers, local Serbs, reservists, who went around the buses and pointed to certain people on the bus. Later these people were taken off the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you were once again met by Serb soldiers, local Serbs and reservists, when you say Serb soldiers, are you including regular soldiers or not in that term?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I didn't see regular soldiers there. I meant the Serb reservists from Serbia and the local Serbs from Vukovar, also wearing uniforms of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Briefly can you tell us what the atmosphere was like at the Vukovar barracks and how you felt emotionally?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The atmosphere was horrendous. The soldiers boarded the buses and beat the people who sat in front. A man was taken off my bus too. They told us that all of us would be executed, they were saying things to us like, "You'll never see Croatia again." They were hurling insults our way, and saying, "All of you would be taken to an execution site and shot." And we felt tremendous fear for our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were on the bus were you looking around the Vukovar military barracks compound to see what was happening with everyone else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The little that I could look around, I could see that the similar things were happening on other buses. That is to say people were pointed out and taken off the buses and led away. Now, as to what happened to them afterwards, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You say the little that you could look around, was there anything stopping you from looking around completely? And, if there was, can you explain?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: We had to sit with our hands on our backs with our heads lowered down so as not to look around, not to look outside. That's what they told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How many people were taken off your bus?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: One person from Zagreb, I believe, was taken off my bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to him once he got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: No, he was simply led away. I didn't see what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the barracks for before you left?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Approximately two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you left the barracks where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Once we left the barracks we stopped in a field in front of a hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what that place was called then, or subsequently did you discover what it was called later?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time what its name was. Later on I learned it was Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When did you learn later that it was -- that place was called Ovcara, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I learned that once I returned from prison, when some graves were already uncovered and when they believed that some Serb civilians had been shot there and that that place was called Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And we'll discuss this a little later, but you left prison in August 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that when the bus that were you on left the Vukovar Hospital there was an armed military police officer on that bus. Was that person still on the bus when you arrived at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes. They accompanied us all the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When your bus arrived at Ovcara can you tell us what you saw whilst you were still seated on the bus? What was happening outside?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Once we arrived at Ovcara we saw people leave the buses in front of us. We saw that the Serbs had lined up two rows of local Serbs and soldiers. As the people got off the buses, they beat them with whatever they got their hands on. So people passed between these two rows and entered the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think that I need to intervene, page 61, line 18 and 19. It seems to me that the witness said that these two rows were composed of local Serb soldiers, and then the transcript reflects local Serbs and soldiers, so could that please be clarified with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that people from the buses had to pass through the two rows. After they passed through those two rows, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The door of the hangar was open, and they took them inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And as you just heard, it's a little bit unclear whether the two rows were local Serb soldiers or local Serbs, or whether or not they were some other regular or reserve or paramilitaries. Can you be clear about who those people were in the two lines?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Those were Serb reservists wearing JNA uniforms. As soon as people got off the buses, they recognised some of those people and they immediately took them aside. They didn't let them inside the hangar, they simply took them aside, based on which I concluded that those were local Serbs wearing JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that it was the reservists, the local Serb reservists that formed the two lines. Other than those soldiers forming those two lines, were there any other soldiers outside of that line-up that was present outside of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were soldiers, yes, who were everywhere around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these other soldiers that weren't in the line-up, are you able to say what type of soldier they were, from a local armed civilian to a reservist to a paramilitary to a regular? Are you able to say which groups that they may have belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Out all of those you mentioned, I can say that all of them were there, including regular JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In total, including the soldiers or the reservists in the line-up, about how many soldiers, no matter what group they came from, were outside of the hangar when the buses arrived there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: That was quite a large group of some perhaps 50 to 60 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can describe just in a little more detail as to how people would walk through these two lines and what would happen to them, if anything, when they went through the two lines?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Once they got off the buses and moved in the direction of the hangar the people who were there armed with chains, bats, rifles, and so on, would beat the people off the buses as they passed through. This was an all-out beating, following which they were pushed inside the hangar. And in the hangar they had to stand facing the wall with their hands on their backs, facing the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: These beatings that were occurring between the two lines, were you watching that from your bus, or from outside of the hangar when you got off your bus?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I managed to see it from the bus too. I saw the people who were in the bus in front of us get off their bus and I could see that as they were getting off they were being hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about you, how did you get off the bus and what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The same thing happened when it was the turn of my bus to disembark. As soon as the people got off, they had to go through the rows of people and were beaten. When it was my turn, I saw Hrkic and Kuscevic stand on the side in front of the door, they stood with an officer and sort of pointed towards the two of us. When it was our turn to approach, they said, "These are those two soldiers." They got off the bus earlier, and they said that they were the JNA soldiers who had been imprisoned in Vukovar, and then they also said that there were two additional soldiers also captured in Vukovar. And then they pointed to us and we were taken aside so that we didn't have to go through the gauntlet of soldiers beating people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So you got off the bus with Dodaj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes, Dodaj Hajdar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the other two soldiers that they were referring to, who were they again?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Samir Hrkic and Petar Kuscevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the four of you were kept in a group outside the hangar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was there any discussion between any one of you in the group and that officer you talked about or any other soldier there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: When they said that they were two additional soldiers and when we got off our bus, they believed them. We gave them information about the units where we did our service, we gave them the names of our superiors, so that right then initially they believed us, that we had indeed been captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you get beaten or not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: No, not at the time. They simply took us aside then. They even gave us some cigarettes, water, and some other refreshments. Those of us who smoked took some cigarettes, and I think that we went to stand under a tree, and we talked to each other. Some active soldiers approached us, and we stood there talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did those soldiers or anyone else soon discover that you were a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Later, when an officer approached us and started talking to us, he asked us about our nationalities. Once we said we were Croats, or rather one of us was an Albanian, he immediately said that we were no prisoners, that we had deserted, that we were military deserters, and that military deserters are normally shot, and that we would be shot too. If we told the truth, then, yes, we stood some chance of saving our skins. He said we would be transferred to Belgrade to the military investigative prison where we would stand trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So the other two, the other two in your group, they were Croats as well as you, and there was the other person, who was an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes. There was an Albanian and, I apologise, Samir Hrkic was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This officer that was speaking to you and told you that you were deserters, can you describe him, and would you be able to state what his rank was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I think that he had a senior rank, but I couldn't describe it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: His physical description, are you able to provide a few details? Say, his height, his build, his age, whether he was balding or had a head of hair?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think he was of medium height, medium build. As far as one could see, he was balding and had greyish hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What about his age?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Middle-aged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that on page 66, line 4 and 5, it doesn't reflect that the witness said that he was balding and had greyish hair. I think it only says that he had greyish hair, but not that he was balding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my line on my screen, it's line 5, said he was balding and had greyish hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honours. I failed to see that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: This officer, was he with -- well, firstly, what type of uniform was he wearing and would you be able to classify him as a regular or reserve officer or some other type?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: He was a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was he with any other officers or any other soldiers that appeared to be with him at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes, there were several officers, a couple of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you mean a couple of extra officers to the one that you were just talking about, or are you talking about two in total?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: No, no. In addition to the one I mentioned. Altogether there were a couple of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you may have answered this already, but are you able to say what rank he had, the main officer that was doing the questioning?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which rank, but it was a senior-ish rank, a senior rank. Whether he was a lieutenant-colonel or a colonel, I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the other -- the other officer that you referred to that was present with him, are you able to -- well, firstly, do you know his name, this other officer, and are you able to describe him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The other one, I wouldn't be able to say what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And as far as a physical description is concerned, are you able to say how old he is -- he was, how tall he was, and what type of build he had, and say the colour of his hair? And if you can't, just say so, but ...

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask that you look at a video, which we'll show you, and Exhibit Number 225.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We have it on Sanction, Your Honours. And I ask that it be played from one minute and 11 seconds to the end of the video, one minute and 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, we're going play this once fully, and if you can take time to have a look at it, and then once you have seen it once, we'll play it again, and when we play it again I'll ask you a couple of questions. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can play the video, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can play the video fully from 1:11 to 1:29, and then we'll go back. We did, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, now the question I have for you, if we -- looking at that video, was there anyone in that video that you saw at Ovcara on the day that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I believe I may have seen one person, but I'm not entirely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we play the video now and if you could stop us at the point of the person that you believe that you may have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I have -- I wasn't looking at the witness then, but he indicated one of the people, and I just ask that it be stopped on that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, just so that we're clear, we're just going to play the video again, and if you can tell us to stop the video as soon as you see the person that you said that you may have seen in Ovcara. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the record, this is at 1 minute 17 seconds point 4 of Exhibit 225. Witness, when you say that you may have seen him at Ovcara, what was he doing at Ovcara, and why do you say that you may have seen him? Why are you not sure?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: The man was there with a group of officers who were there. And it sounds familiar, but I couldn't say that I am 100 per cent sure that this is precisely that person. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement -- thank you, we've finished with the video now. In the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1996 you stated that the officer that was speaking to you about being a deserter was a General Panic, and you also stated that his junior, or the person that was with him, was a person called Mrksic. In this video we have a -- an officer called Panic in this video. Bearing in mind that you didn't recognise this Panic in this video, are you confident that you identified this Panic to the investigators correctly as the officer that spoke to you about desertion?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It could be that I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Both of these people that were speaking to you, or the officer that was speaking to you about being a deserter, and the other officer that was with him, had you ever seen those people before at Ovcara -- before, before Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You didn't know their names; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you identified two people, namely Panic and Mrksic, to the investigator in 1996, did you tell them, did you tell that investigator their names, or did the investigator tell you their names of the people that you identified?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: When I pointed to these two people, I didn't know who they were, what their names were. The investigator later told me who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how long was this officer speaking to you for, and about how long were you at Ovcara in total?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I spent about half an hour at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst you were at Ovcara did any other person or people arrive there whilst you were standing outside of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: While the four of us were there with some other JNA soldiers, at one point I saw Mr. Sljivancanin arriving. He talked to these people, the Serb reservists, who were in the gauntlet beating people. He said something to them, they talked briefly about something, and then he turned around and left shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was he trying to stop people from being beaten, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: I was hoping that he was somebody who issued an order that people not be beaten, but soon after he left the beating continued, based on which I didn't get the impression that he ordered that people not be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How did Sljivancanin arrive at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: He arrived in a military vehicle, I believe it was a Pinzgauer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he arrive with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Driver brought him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that he left shortly thereafter. About how long did Sljivancanin stay at Ovcara for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: When he arrived he talked to people and he may have stayed five to 10 minutes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would like to show you a video, and it's Exhibit 285. And I would like to play the first six seconds, please. And can you tell us whether you recognise anyone in that video. Or perhaps if we just leave it at the commencement of the video, at zero seconds. Looking at that, that picture, is there anyone in that picture that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mr. Sljivancanin, the person behind the man in white. The person whose head we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that person -- is that person wearing anything or not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Looking from here, I can't really say. I can see his cap, I can see the cap on his head. Now, as to what else he may have on, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were at Ovcara did you see what was happening inside of the hangar, all of the detainees that were taken in there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: There were soldiers entering the hangar at will. It was dreadful how those people inside were beaten. Every now and then they would recognise someone, the local Serbs, I mean. They would take them outside the hangar, behind the hangar, and I have no idea what became of those people. For the most part they would go into the hangar and beat people unconscious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you left Ovcara, were you taken to Negoslavci where you were detained for three or four days?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who detained you, and were you beaten whilst you were detained?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA
utterances.text: We were in a cellar. When we reached Negoslavci we were all blindfolded and taken down to a basement of sorts, and they started beating us there. It was horrendous. Local Serbs would appear, saying that we should all be killed and that they would kill all of us, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a maximum of 10 minutes left, perhaps it would only be five. I am happy to continue on now or, alternatively, first thing tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it that's a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Tomorrow we resume in the morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of June, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.59 p.m.,
